title: UV Index, SPF and MED: How Much Sunscreen Actually Blocks
h1: UV index, SPF, MED — the sunscreen math dermatologists use
description: SPF 30 blocks 96.7% of UVB, SPF 50 blocks 98%. UV Index 8 gives a fair-skinned person sunburn in ~15 min unprotected. Here is how the numbers combine.

hero: The UV Index is a normalized scale where 1 unit = 25 mW/m² of erythemally weighted UV. SPF is a multiplier on your Minimum Erythemal Dose (MED). Combine them and you get exactly how long you can stay in the sun before pink turns to burn.
body: The WHO/WMO UV Index (UVI) is a dimensionless number: UVI = weighted UV irradiance (W/m²) × 40. UVI 10 therefore equals 250 mW/m² of erythema-weighted UV — the CIE-84 action spectrum that reddens human skin. Sunscreen SPF is defined by ISO 24444:2019 as the ratio of protected-skin MED to unprotected-skin MED, measured on Fitzpatrick I–III volunteers with 2 mg/cm² applied. Real-world SPF is usually one-half to one-third of label because people apply 0.5–1 mg/cm².
## The exact numbers

> UV Index: 1 UVI = 25 mW/m² erythemal irradiance (WHO 2002)
> SPF n blocks 1 − 1/n of UVB: SPF 15 = 93.3%, SPF 30 = 96.7%, SPF 50 = 98.0%, SPF 100 = 99.0%
> Time-to-burn (protected) = MED / (erythemal irradiance × (1 − block%))
> Fair skin (type II) MED ≈ 250 J/m²; medium (type IV) ≈ 450 J/m²; dark (type VI) ≈ 1000 J/m²
## UV Index vs sunburn time (unprotected, Fitzpatrick II)

| UVI | Category (WHO) | Time to redness | Time to first-degree burn |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | Low | 60+ min | 4+ hours |
| 3–5 | Moderate | 30–45 min | 1–2 h |
| 6–7 | High | 20–25 min | 45 min |
| 8–10 | Very High | 12–15 min | 25 min |
| 11+ | Extreme | 8–10 min | 15 min |
## Adding sunscreen to the math

SPF multiplies the safe window. Fair-skinned person, UVI 8, SPF 30 correctly applied: 15 min × 30 = 7.5 hours before burn — if reapplied every 2 hours, no water, no sweat. Real-world halving: cut it to 3.7 hours. Same person under-applies to 1 mg/cm²: effective SPF drops to ~SPF 8 (per Petersen & Wulf, *Photodermatol Photoimmunol Photomed* 2014), so 15 × 8 = 2 hours to burn.
## Worked example — beach day, UVI 10
Person: fair skin (Fitzpatrick II, MED ≈ 250 J/m²). UVI 10 = 250 mW/m². Unprotected time to MED: 250 / 0.250 = 1000 s ≈ 17 min.

> With SPF 50, 2 mg/cm² applied: blocks 98%. Effective irradiance 5 mW/m². Time to MED = 250 / 0.005 = 50 000 s ≈ 14 h.
> Reality: SPF 50 applied at 1 mg/cm² performs at ~SPF 15. Blocks 93%. Time to MED = 250 / 0.0175 = 14 300 s ≈ 4 h.
> After swimming/sweating: reapply every 80 min (ISO 24444 water-resistant claim = tested for 40 min immersion twice).
## Why SPF 100 is not '2× SPF 50'

Diminishing returns: SPF 50 blocks 98.0%, SPF 100 blocks 99.0% — one extra percentage point of UVB. Where SPF 100 does help: photosensitive skin (lupus, drug-induced), high-altitude/snow (UVI 12+), and people who habitually under-apply. The FDA proposed capping labels at 'SPF 60+' in 2019 to reduce false confidence; the rule is not yet finalized.
## UVA vs UVB

SPF measures UVB (290–320 nm), which causes acute sunburn. UVA (320–400 nm) penetrates deeper, causes tanning, photoaging, and contributes to melanoma. UVA protection is measured by PPD (Japan/EU) or the 'broad spectrum' pass/fail (US FDA). Look for: PA++++ (Asia), UVA circle logo (EU, PPD ≥ SPF/3), or 'Broad Spectrum SPF 30+' (US).
## Altitude, water, snow amplification

UV rises ~10% per 1000 m elevation (Blumthaler et al., *Ambio* 1997). At 4000 m, UVI 8 at sea level becomes UVI ~12. Water reflects 10–30% (rough water reflects less than mirror-flat), fresh snow 80–90%, dry sand 15–20%. Skiing on a UVI 5 mountain day gets effective UVI ~9 on your face.
## Clothing and shade

UPF (Ultraviolet Protection Factor) works the same way as SPF: UPF 50 blocks 98% of UV. A dry cotton white T-shirt is ~UPF 5–7; wet drops to UPF 3. Rated swim shirts (Coolibar, Patagonia sun hoody) claim UPF 50+. Umbrella shade cuts direct UV by 50–75% but not scattered sky UV — beach umbrella + sunscreen is standard because either alone is insufficient at UVI 8+.
## Vitamin D trade-off

Full-body noon exposure at UVI 3+ for ~10 min (light skin) or 25 min (dark skin) produces ~1000 IU vitamin D (Holick, *NEJM* 2007). Beyond that dose, D synthesis plateaus while burn risk continues to climb. Sunscreen SPF 30 reduces D synthesis by <5% in real use because coverage is imperfect — the 'sunscreen causes deficiency' claim is not supported by clinical data.
## The five-second recap
UVI × 25 = mW/m². SPF n blocks (1 − 1/n) of UVB. Time-to-burn (unprotected) × SPF = protected time, halved for real-world application. Reapply every 2 hours or after swimming.

faqs.a: About 1 oz (30 mL, a shot glass) for a full adult body, or ~1/2 tsp for face + neck. Most people apply 25–50% of that dose, which is why label SPF exceeds real SPF by 2–4×.
ISO 24444: SPF retained after two 20-min immersions with 20-min rest between. 'Water resistant 40 min' = one immersion cycle. Neither is 'waterproof' — that word was banned by the FDA in 2011.

Yes — WHO UVI is instantaneous erythemal irradiance from actual measurement or model. Peak UVI is 11 AM–3 PM in summer. Weather-app UVI is usually clear-sky forecast; cloud cover reduces UV by 10–50% but thin cloud can *increase* it (broken cumulus reflection).

faqs.q: Do phone camera lenses work for UV?
faqs.a: No — glass and standard sensors filter UV below 380 nm. Consumer 'UV camera' apps read the UVI feed from weather APIs; they do not measure.

faqs.q: SPF for melasma or scar prevention?
faqs.a: Dermatologists recommend SPF 50+ broad-spectrum daily for melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and scar prevention, plus iron-oxide-containing tint for visible-light protection (VL contributes to pigmentation in Fitzpatrick IV–VI).
